hints: Notice the word only - test each of diffraction, interference, polarisation and reflection against both transverse and longitudinal waves.
Recall that in a transverse wave oscillations are perpendicular to propagation, while in a longitudinal wave oscillations are parallel to propagation.
Ask which effect requires selecting one plane of oscillation - sound from a loudspeaker cannot be filtered this way but light through a Polaroid can.
walkthrough: Identify the wave types: transverse waves have displacement perpendicular to energy travel, longitudinal waves have displacement parallel to energy travel.

Check diffraction, interference and reflection: sound, which is longitudinal, can diffract through doorways, interfere from two speakers, and reflect as an echo, so these are not exclusive to transverse waves.
Consider polarisation: it means limiting the vibrations to a single plane perpendicular to the direction of propagation.
A longitudinal wave has only one line of vibration along its propagation direction, so there is no plane to select and it cannot be polarised.
A transverse wave can vibrate in many directions perpendicular to propagation, so one direction can be selected by a polariser.
Therefore polarisation is only associated with transverse waves. This is option C

options.A: Diffraction is spreading through a gap or around an obstacle and occurs for both transverse waves like light and longitudinal waves like sound.
options.B: Interference is superposition of coherent waves to give reinforcement and cancellation and occurs for both transverse and longitudinal waves.
options.C: Polarisation restricts oscillations to one plane perpendicular to propagation, which is only possible when oscillations are transverse to the direction of travel.
options.D: Reflection is bouncing at a boundary and occurs for both transverse waves and longitudinal waves such as sound echoes.
